analysis.one_liner: Extends credit-sale fee caps, price disclosures, and debt-collection protections to rent-to-own customers.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 15 cosponsors including one Republican, was referred to the House Banking Committee and a subcommittee in late 1997 and never received a markup, a vote, or a floor hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated rent-to-own contracts like other consumer credit sales: capping fees and charges at the levels state law allows for installment sales, requiring stores to post the cash price, annual percentage rate, and total cost to own each item, and applying federal lending, discrimination, debt collection, and credit reporting laws to these deals. It would have let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules and let customers sue for damages. Rent-to-own contracts are mostly used by low-income households to acquire furniture and appliances, and the bill's findings state the industry targets low-income and minority neighborhoods.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers, who are disproportionately low-income and minority households buying furniture, appliances, and electronics without access to conventional credit. They would have gained the right to see the true cash price and total cost of ownership up front, protection from abusive collection tactics like threats of criminal prosecution, and the right to sue dealers for violations with statutory damages of $250 for disclosure failures and $2,500 for other violations.

how_it_helps.text: Caps rent-to-own interest, finance charges, and fees at what state law allows for a credit or installment sale of the same item, and extends state warranty protections to rent-to-own goods.
Requires stores to post and disclose in writing the cash price, annual percentage rate, payment amounts, total payments needed to own the item, and whether it is new or used.
Applies four federal consumer laws to rent-to-own deals: the Truth in Lending Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
Bars dealers from threatening criminal prosecution, using threats or coercion to collect, harassing customers, or unreasonably disclosing debts to third parties.
Makes the Federal Trade Commission the enforcer and lets customers sue for actual damages plus $250 per disclosure failure or $2,500 per other violation, with attorney fees.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers, whose profit margins depend on charges well above the cash price of the merchandise. They would face new disclosure obligations, caps on fees and credit insurance premiums, federal collection and lending rules, FTC enforcement, and civil liability. Some costs would likely be passed to customers through higher prices or reduced availability of rent-to-own plans.

drawbacks.text: The fee cap only works where state law caps installment-sale charges. In states with no such caps, section 1004 sets no ceiling, so rent-to-own rates would remain uncapped there.
The bill lets dealers charge a termination fee of up to 5 percent of the cash price and recovery fees for goods not returned, adding costs for customers who end a contract early.

Compliance and liability costs could push some dealers to raise prices, cut services, or exit markets, reducing access for customers who rely on rent-to-own because they cannot qualify for conventional credit.
It preempts state rent-to-own laws to the extent they conflict with the federal scheme, replacing some state rules with a federal floor rather than adding to them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the low-income customers the bill targets, the benefits are concrete: seeing the true total cost before signing, protection from threats and harassment, and a private right to sue. The costs fall on dealers and partly on customers through prices, and the design has real weaknesses: the fee cap imports state caps rather than setting a federal one, leaving customers in states with weak caps little protection. On balance, the protections address practices the bill itself documents as widespread, and the preserve-the-termination-right structure is more moderate than an outright rate cap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Banking Committee and its consumer credit subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Kennedy II of Massachusetts introduced the bill on November 13, 1997, joined by 15 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 1 Republican.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services.
On December 13, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it stayed.
No markup, hearing, or vote is recorded in the action history, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers are better off because the bill died: they kept operating without federal fee caps, price disclosures, or collection restrictions, and their customers kept paying whatever the contracts charged.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only partisan signal is sponsorship, which was 14 Democrats and 1 Republican.

industries.note: Rent-to-own dealers' revenue depends on charges far above the cash price of merchandise, and the bill would cap those charges at state installment-sale levels, mandate price disclosure, and expose dealers to FTC enforcement and lawsuits. Its own findings state the industry targets low-income and minority neighborhoods, so the burden of the current pricing model falls on those customers.

The bill would limit rent-to-own dealers to the types and premium amounts of credit insurance state law allows for installment sales, cutting into credit insurance premiums bundled into these contracts.
